stances.claim: Despite the pessimism of many Filipinos, the World Bank's confident answer is yes -- the Philippines can eradicate poverty within one generation provided the economy sustains 6 percent annual growth, which would raise per capita income from $3,300 in 2013 to $35,000 by 2043

Singapore-China-Malaysia have demonstrated poverty eradication is achievable, but the usual objection is that this came 'at the cost of freedom' -- Time magazine documented Lee Kuan Yew's suppression of dissent, press freedom curbs, and micromanagement extending to chewing gum bans, marriage-pushing, childbirth limits, and toilet-flush rules

To be fair, Lee Kuan Yew led by example -- modest living, stopped communist insurgency, jailed the corrupt, paid public servants higher than private sector, rewarded meritocracy -- making Singapore one of the best places to live, especially now that controls on speech have eased

To eradicate poverty within a generation, the Philippines need not ape Singapore or China -- per the WB's 'Making Growth Work for the Poor,' what matters is investing in health/education/infrastructure, enhancing competition, simplifying regulations, and protecting property rights

WB president Jim Yong Kim -- whom CJP met personally -- boldly announced the Bank's twin goals of ending extreme poverty by 2030 and boosting shared prosperity among the poorest 40 percent in developing countries, without any mention of altering political systems

Authoritarianism -- whether Chinese or Singaporean variety -- will not work in the Philippines: after our sad experience under Marcos, the people will not allow a return to one-party or one-man rule; martial law's discipline gave way to corruption and cronyism unlike Singapore's intelligent and selfless leadership

Authoritarian rule has become outmoded everywhere -- in the Information Age, suppression is no longer possible; the Internet defies territorial boundaries; the ICC prosecutes despots across borders; voluntary arbitration breaks judicial-tribunal monopolies -- Filipinos will just work together in freedom

As CJP said in his recent Asean Law Association speech: peoples differ in histories, traditions, cultures, ideologies, and mindsets, but all need liberty and prosperity; some start with economic-first-then-liberty, some with liberty-first, some both at once -- but eventually and inevitably, all peoples need and deserve liberty and prosperity in equal measure

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes for Labor Day a foundational FLP economic-philosophy column asking: Will our government ever be able to eradicate poverty? Despite the pessimism of many Filipinos, the World Bank's confident answer is yes -- within one generation, provided the economy sustains its current 6 percent annual growth. The math is striking: at this rate, the Philippines can double per capita income in a decade, raise it five times in two decades, and 11 times in three decades -- average yearly per capita income of $3,300 in 2013 would increase to $35,000 in 2043. Singapore, China, and Malaysia have done it. The usual objection is that they eradicated poverty 'at the cost of freedom.' As Time magazine (April 6, 2015) noted, Lee Kuan Yew -- who died March 23 after serving as PM from 1959 to 1990 and 'mentor' thereafter -- trumped the individual in favor of the community: suppressing dissent, jailing oppositors, curbing press freedom, and micromanaging life to the extent of banning chewing gum (to prevent littering), pushing the educated elite to marry one another (to upgrade the people's genes), limiting childbirth (to control population), and telling everyone to flush toilets (to prevent diseases). To be fair, however, LKY led by example in living modestly, stopped communist insurgency, jailed the corrupt, paid public servants higher than the private sector, and rewarded meritocracy -- making Singapore one of the best places to live, especially now that it has eased speech controls. To eradicate poverty within a generation, must the Philippines ape Singapore or China? Not necessarily, says the WB. What matters per its paper 'Making Growth Work for the Poor' is investing more in health, education, and infrastructure, enhancing competition, simplifying regulations, and protecting property rights -- validated by international aid agencies, think tanks, and credible local economists like Romeo Bernardo and business leaders like Ramon del Rosario. WB president Jim Yong Kim -- whom CJP met personally during his recent PH visit -- boldly announced the Bank's twin goals: ending extreme poverty in the world by 2030 (only half a generation from now) and boosting shared prosperity among the poorest 40 percent in developing countries, without any mention of altering political systems. Authoritarianism, whether Chinese or Singaporean variety, will not work in the Philippines. After the sad experience under Marcos, the people will not allow a return to one-party or one-man rule. True, many cheered the discipline and respite from chaos that martial law brought during its first few years, but later on corruption and cronyism crept in -- unlike Singapore where the leadership was intelligent, single-minded, selfless, and honest. Authoritarian rule has become outmoded -- not just in Asia but in the old Soviet republics, the Middle East, South America, and Africa -- yes, in the whole world. Suppression of individual freedom is no longer possible in the Information Age: the Internet and digital transmission cannot be confined by traditional sovereign and territorial boundaries; despots can no longer hide their crimes; serious offenses can be prosecuted across borders via the ICC; commercial and civil disputes are no longer the monopoly of judicial tribunals because parties can now choose laws and judges through voluntary arbitration. Yes, we Filipinos will just have to work together in freedom to continue the reforms in good governance and the economy. CJ closes with his FLP signature passage from a recent Asean Law Association speech: 'The peoples of the world and of Asean have different histories, traditions, cultures, ideologies and mindsets. But I dare say all of them need liberty and prosperity. Some countries... start with improving their people's economic lives first and restrict temporarily in measured stages their political liberty. Some others begin with political liberty thinking that their economy would flourish as a necessary consequence. Still some others rise with a combination of both liberty and prosperity at the very beginning... But I also firmly believe that eventually and inevitably, all the peoples of the world need and deserve liberty and prosperity in equal measure.'
